newsitem.title: USA: BASEBALL-MODEST HOMERS PRODUCE BIG RUNS IN RANGERS' WIN.
newsitem.headline: BASEBALL-MODEST HOMERS PRODUCE BIG RUNS IN RANGERS' WIN.

text.p: Neither ball left the bat with a solid thunk, but both quickly assumed a lethal trajectory -- high and headed for the leftfield corner -- and both carried just far enough to lift the Rangers to a playoff win over the New York Yankees.

The fourth-inning homers by strong men Juan Gonzalez and Dean Palmer were modest by major league standards. But the five runs they produced off Yankees ace David Cone were huge as Texas took a 6-2 win in Tuesday's opener of their dvisional series.
"I'm upset. I have no excuses," said Cone. "That was an unbelievable inning."
Yankee Stadium is a ball park known for far-reaching fences that have thwarted power-hitting righthanded batters over the decades.
Renovations over the years have shrunk the left-centre power alley to a still formidable 399 feet and centre field remains a daunting distance of 408 feet.

But down the line is sublime for sluggers and Gonzalez, who muscled out an inside fastball, and Palmer, who pounced on a hanging curve, played the angles to perfection and took advantage of the inviting 318-foot porch in the corner.
After Ivan Rodriguez singled and Rusty Greer walked to lead off the fourth, Gonzalez, who smashed 47 homers and drove in 144 runs this year, cleared the fence with a clout that measured 321 feet.
Will Clark then singled to set the stage for Palmer, who pounded 38 home runs and had 107 RBI this season. His two-run homer that capped off the big inning covered a grand total of 325 feet.
"It's one of the biggest hits of my career," said Gonzalez. "I just turned on it. I didn't hit it that hard."
Asked if he was worried that his drive that put Texas ahead 3-1 would hook foul, Gonzalez said: "No. I didn't hit it hard enough."
Palmer, who also made a brilliant stop of a first-inning smash by Paul O'Neill to save at least one run, said: "I think he just left a few pitches up and we took advantage."
Yankees manager Joe Torre said Cone got in trouble when he lost his location after three brilliant innings of work.
"The thing about Texas, you make a mistake, it's not a single. It's a home run."
